Systems-Over-Goals.title: Systems Over Goals
Systems-Over-Goals.content:
Systems Over Goals for AI-Managed Knowledge Bases
Build sustainable automated capture and processing systems rather than chasing outcome-based goals.
The Core Rule

Rule: Design knowledge management systems that run continuously rather than pursuing milestone-based objectives.
Why: Goals are binary (achieved or not) and discourage continued effort after completion. Systems are continuous and always actionable, leading to compounding growth. AI agents excel at sustained automated operations.
Test: Can your knowledge management system run unattended? Does it process captures automatically, or does it require manual intervention to “complete” a phase?

The Problem with Goals in KB Automation
Goals have issues in automated contexts:

Binary: achieved or failed, no middle ground
Completion triggers idle periods until next goal is set
Hard to measure progress in continuous operation
Don’t leverage AI’s strength in sustained repetitive tasks

The Power of Systems in KB Automation
Systems are different for AI agents:

Continuous: operates 24/7 without milestone dependency
Automated: processes captures without human initiation
Measurable: flow rate, processing latency, quality metrics
Compoundable: each cycle improves the next

Examples: Goals vs Systems

























Goal-Based ApproachSystem-Based Approach”Add 100 notes on topic X”Continuous capture pipeline processing all relevant inputs”Complete vault structure”Ongoing structural health monitoring and repair”Finish linking phase”Automatic link suggestion and verification on each capture”Reach 50% coverage”Continuous frontier exploration with diminishing-returns gating
The Knowledge Management System
For AI agents:
Instead of “process all notes in inbox”:

Continuous inbox monitoring with 48-hour SLA processing
Auto-categorization and tagging on capture
Link suggestion run on each new note

Instead of “achieve complete linking”:

Link quality scoring on each connection
Orphan detection running as background process
Hub distribution monitored continuously

Instead of “reach maturity”:

Diminishing returns testing on each addition
Quality signal tracking over time
Explicit completion criteria per domain

System Architecture Components

Capture Pipeline - Automatic ingestion and initial processing
Link Engine - Continuous relationship discovery
Health Monitor - Structural integrity tracking
Quality Gate - Diminishing returns testing before addition
Frontier Scanner - Active gap discovery

The Shift
Goal: “Process all backlog notes”
System: “Inbox monitored continuously with automatic escalation”
Goal: “Achieve perfect structure”
System: “Structural health scored on each operation, repair triggered on degradation”
Goal: “Complete domain coverage”
System: “Diminishing returns test applied to each potential addition”

The-Extended-Mind.title: The Extended Mind
The-Extended-Mind.content:
The Extended Mind
Your second brain as an extension of your biological mind.
The Cognitive Limit
Human cognition has boundaries:

Working memory: 7±2 items
Long-term storage: Large but finite
Retrieval: Imperfect and slow

The solution: Externalize and network.
The Extended Mind Thesis
Just as telescopes extend vision and computers extend computation:

Notes extend memory
Links extend association
Search extends recall
AI extends insight

Your mind + networked tools = the extended mind.
Three Metaphors for the Same Truth
1. The Modular Mind (Offloading)
Store what your brain shouldn’t memorize:

Facts, formulas, references
Free cognitive resources for thinking
“Google for your own mind”

Benefits:

Offload — Don’t memorize what you can retrieve
Extend — Access more than biological limits allow
Accelerate — Instant search and structured linking

2. The Networked Mind (Connecting)
The whole is greater than the sum:

Connections reveal insights you’d miss
Graph traversal beats linear recall
Emergence happens at the network level

The shift from:

Brain stores everything → Brain + network
Limited by skull → Limited by network

3. The Operating System (Integration)
Your second brain manages knowledge resources:
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│      Knowledge OS              │
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Input    →  Storage  →  Output │
│  Capture  →  Connect  →  Act    │
│  Learn    →  Emerge   →  Create│
└─────────────────────────────────┘

Benefits:

Resource Management — Know what you know
Parallel Processing — Work with multiple ideas
Error Correction — Update outdated thinking
Bootstrapping — New knowledge builds on old

The API Analogy
Your knowledge base works like an API:

Input — Books, articles, conversations → notes
Processing — Atomic notes, connections, emergence
Output — Insights, decisions, creations

This creates consistency, scalability, and integration.
The Hybrid Model
Combine biological and external cognition:

























Biological BrainSecond BrainCreativityStorageJudgmentRetrievalInsightStructureScale
Best practice: Don’t over-rely on external (atrophies recall) or under-rely (wastes cognitive resources). Let each do what it does best.
The Learning Stack
A Learning Stack is your integrated system for building knowledge infrastructure. It provides the practical layers that implement the Extended Mind concepts:
The Five Layers



































LayerFunctionActivitiesCaptureQuick inputVoice memos, clipping, inboxProcessingNote creationAtomic notes, linking, templatingStorageOrganizationSecond brain, graph, searchReviewMaintenanceSpaced repetition, weekly reviewsOutputValue creationWriting, teaching, decisions
Layer Integration
All layers connect in a flow:

Input flows through capture → process → storage
Review maintains quality
Output creates feedback that fuels new input

This creates a virtuous cycle of knowledge growth. Each layer reinforces the others:

Capture feeds Processing (raw material → structured notes)
Processing feeds Storage (atomic notes → graph)
Storage feeds Review (material available for maintenance)
Review feeds Output (well-maintained knowledge → insights)
Output feeds new Capture (sharing generates questions and responses)

The Future
AI assistants will increasingly:

Query your knowledge automatically
Find connections you miss
Surface insights proactively

Your second brain is the foundation. The network amplifies it.

The-Forgetting-Curve.title: The Forgetting Curve
The-Forgetting-Curve.content:
The Forgetting Curve and Its Implications
Understanding memory decay to optimize your second brain.
The Science (Ebbinghaus, 1885)
Hermann Ebbinghaus discovered that information decays rapidly:

25% remembered after 1 day
33% remembered after 2 days
28% remembered after 6 days
25% remembered after 31 days

This is the forgetting curve.
The Implications for Knowledge Management
1. Review Timing
Review notes BEFORE forgetting:

First review: 1 day after creating
Second review: 3 days later
Third review: 7 days later
Fourth review: 14 days later
Fifth review: 30 days later

This is the basis of spaced repetition (see Review Timing).
2. Active Engagement
Passive re-reading does little. Active retrieval is key:

Close your notes and try to recall
Test yourself with flashcards
Apply concepts to new situations

How to Practice Retrieval
The most effective learning technique is forcing yourself to recall information.
1. Flashcards

Convert atomic notes to flashcards
Use spaced repetition (see spaced repetition schedule)
Focus on connections, not just facts

2. Closed-Book Notes

Try to write from memory
Check against your notes
Fill gaps

3. Teaching

Explain a concept without looking
The Feynman Technique
Identify gaps in understanding

4. Practice Problems

Apply concepts to new scenarios
Test understanding, not just recall

Common Retrieval Mistakes

Passive reading — Just highlighting = no learning
Too soon — Retrieval after 5 minutes < retrieval after 1 day
Too easy — Don’t use multiple choice; use free recall

3. Meaningful Connections
Links in your graph provide retrieval cues:

When you see a related note, it triggers recall
More connections = more retrieval paths
This is why Linking Principle matters

4. Regular Maintenance
Per Self-Improvement Cycle and Graph Maintenance:

Review notes before they go stale
Update outdated information
Strengthen weak connections

Counteracting the Curve

























FactorEffectMeaningful encodingSlower decaySpaced reviewExtends retentionActive retrievalStrengthens memoryMultiple contextsRicher encoding
Active vs Passive Retention
In a second brain system, retention happens through two mechanisms:
Passive Retention:

Well-linked notes are easier to find later
Graph structure surfaces related concepts
Search and backlinks enable rediscovery

Active Retention:

Spaced repetition review
Writing notes in your own words (encoding)
Teaching concepts to others (elaboration)
Cross-domain connections (interleaving)

Knowledge Base Application

Create notes with strong connections (more retrieval cues)
Review systematically using spaced repetition
Update regularly to reinforce memory
Link extensively to create retrieval network

Retrieval in Your Knowledge Base

Review sessions - Close notes, try to reconstruct
Flashcard creation - From atomic notes
Quiz yourself - Use Dataview to generate questions
Teach others - Share knowledge to verify

Tools for Practice
Popular spaced repetition systems put this science into practice:

Anki — flashcard software with spaced repetition
SuperMemo — implements the SM-2 algorithm
RemNote — combines note-taking with SR

The-Innovation-Engine.title: The Innovation Engine
The-Innovation-Engine.content:
The Innovation Engine
Using your knowledge base to generate new ideas through connections.
The Combination Principle

Innovation = combination of existing ideas

Three combination types drive innovation:

























TypeDescriptionExampleNew + NewNovel synthesisTwo recent research papers combine into new hypothesisExisting + ExistingCross-domain connectionCooking technique applied to chemistryNew + ExistingApplicationNew technology applied to existing problem
How Knowledge Bases Enable Innovation
1. Serendipity (Passive)
Notes from different domains connect unexpectedly:

Read note A (domain X)
Read note B (domain Y)
Hidden connection emerges

Enable: Maintain diverse notes across multiple domains
2. Deliberate Combination (Active)
Seek connections intentionally:

Ask: “How does X apply to Y?”
Search existing notes for patterns
Force combination across domains

Enable: Regular cross-domain note review
3. External Trigger (Reactive)
New input activates existing knowledge:

New book + existing notes
Problem + existing solutions
Conversation + accumulated knowledge

Enable: Capture triggers immediately, link to existing knowledge
The Innovation Process

Build diverse knowledge — Cover multiple domains
Let connections emerge — Read across domains regularly
Deliberately seek combinations — Ask cross-domain questions
Document new insights — Create notes from emergent ideas

Concrete Techniques
Interleaving
Mix topics during review sessions to find unexpected connections. See Interleaving.
Cross-Domain Questions
Ask: “What would [domain X expert] say about [domain Y problem]?”
Analogical Transfer
Explicitly ask: “How does [concept A] mirror [concept B]?”

The-Inverse-Test.title: The Inverse Test
The-Inverse-Test.content:
The Inverse Test

A technique for discovering undocumented knowledge boundaries — companion to Types of Applicability Boundaries

The Method
For any absolute statement (always/never/every/none), ask inverse questions:

“Always? Under what conditions?”
“Never? In what contexts?”
“What would make this false?”

If you can’t answer, the boundary may be undocumented.
Why It Works
Absolute statements imply universal applicability. But most knowledge has boundaries. The inverse test exposes them.
Examples





















Absolute ClaimInverse Questions”Never use recursion”Except when? For what problem sizes?”Always verify sources”Except for well-known facts? Common knowledge?”Every note needs 3+ links”What about new notes? Foundational concepts?
When to Apply

When writing new notes with absolute language
When reviewing notes for completeness
When testing if a domain has well-documented boundaries

The Knowledge Creator
Turning consumption into creation through structured practice.
From Passive to Active
Most people consume knowledge passively:

The-Last-Skill.title: The Last Skill
The-Last-Skill.content:
The Last Skill
The meta-skill that makes all others easier.

Rule: Treat learning how to learn as a skill to be actively developed, not a passive ability.
Why: Meta-learning skills compound across all domains — investing in them provides returns everywhere.
Test: Can you explain your learning process for a recent topic? Do you have a system for improving how you acquire, organize, and use knowledge?

What Is “The Last Skill”?
Learning how to learn:

Knowing how to acquire knowledge
Knowing how to organize knowledge
Knowing how to use knowledge

Your second brain IS this skill made concrete.
Why It’s Last
Other skills have limits:

Coding: specific to programs
Writing: specific to text
Speaking: specific to audio

The last skill underlies all:

Every field needs knowledge
Every profession learns
Everyone needs to think

First-Principles Thinking
The knowledge base also enables first-principles thinking — breaking down problems to fundamentals, questioning assumptions, and rebuilding from scratch.

First principles combine to form new first principles
This is how original thinking happens

The-Ownership-Mindset.title: The Ownership Mindset
The-Ownership-Mindset.content:
The Ownership Mindset
Taking full responsibility for your knowledge — and letting it transform who you are.
The Core Rule

Rule: Own the curation, processing, and structure of your knowledge — don’t delegate it to external sources or tools.
Why: Knowledge you passively consume from others lacks personal context and compounding value. Ownership ensures knowledge serves your specific needs and grows with your understanding.
Test: Can you trace every note in your vault to your own curation decision? Do you have notes that are purely copied content without personal synthesis?

The Mindset Shift
Before: Knowledge happens to you

Take courses someone else designed
Read books someone else recommended
Learn what “they” say is important
Rely on memory → forget connections
Single-track thinking → isolated ideas
Passive consumption → knowledge loss

After: You own your learning

Design your own curriculum
Connect what matters to you
Build your own knowledge
External thinking partner → always available
Multi-track connections → network thoughts
Active synthesis → new insights emerge

Behavioral Markers
A knowledge identity shows up in concrete actions:





















BeforeAfter”I forgot where I read that""It’s in my notes, let me link it""Those two ideas might connect""Let me create a note linking them""I need to remember this""I need to capture and process this”
Ownership Actions
1. Curate Your Inputs

Choose what to consume
Don’t just follow trends

2. Process Actively

Don’t just save - understand
Write in your own words

3. Build Your Structure

Create your own categories
Link what makes sense to you
Don’t copy others’ structures

4. Share Your Perspective

Add your interpretation
Don’t just regurgitate
Build on others’ ideas

The Creation Pipeline

See The Knowledge Creator for the full pipeline details.
The core framework: Input → Process → Create → Share
Ownership means completing all four stages rather than stopping at consumption.

Why Create?
Taking ownership leads to tangible benefits:

Deeper learning - Teaching forces synthesis
Reputation - Build credibility through demonstrated knowledge
Impact - Help others accelerate their learning
Income - Monetize specialized knowledge

Test: Can you point to one concrete benefit you’ve received from creating knowledge?
How the Seed Enables This
The Seed rules create the infrastructure for ownership and identity:

Atomic Note Principle — Single ideas are combinable
Linking Principle — Every connection is explicit
Graph Traversal Efficiency — Ideas are always reachable
Self-Improvement Cycle — The system evolves with you

Measuring Your Growth
Test questions:

Can you trace every note in your vault to your own curation decision?
Can you trace any idea back to its sources?
Do you instinctively link new inputs to existing notes?
When you learn something new, do you ask “where does this fit?”
Do you have notes that are purely copied content without personal synthesis?

The Transformation
Your second brain becomes part of who you are:

How you process — Always adding to the graph
How you decide — Evidence from notes, not just memory
How you create — Recombine atomic notes into new insights

Why It Matters
When you own your knowledge:

You remember more
You think better
You create more
You stand out

AI-Specific Ownership
In an AI-assisted knowledge base, ownership means:

Prompt Ownership - Your capture prompts reflect your thinking style, not generic templates
Linking Philosophy - You decide how concepts connect, not just what links exist
Synthesis Direction - You guide what insights emerge, not just what gets captured
Quality Standards - You define what makes a note valuable for your context

An AI can generate notes, but only you can provide the personal context that makes them valuable.

Tool-Replacement-Decisions.title: Tool Replacement Decisions
Tool-Replacement-Decisions.content:
Tool Replacement Decisions
When to switch knowledge management tools vs. when to migrate content.
The Core Question
You’ve invested time building knowledge in one tool. When does it make sense to switch tools rather than continue with the current one?
Decision Framework
Stay If:

Current tool meets 80%+ of needs
Migration cost > improvement gain
Lock-in is acceptable (export available)
Workflow is established and productive

Switch If:

Tool is abandoned or unmaintained
Fundamental limitations prevent core workflows
Data export is becoming impossible (format changes)
Security/privacy requirements change fundamentally

Migrate Content If:

New tool has better structure for your evolved needs
Old tool format is degrading (bit rot, format obsolescence)
You’re starting fresh with new methodology

Cost-Benefit Analysis






























FactorStaySwitchTime to migrate0HighLearning curveLowHighWorkflow disruptionNoneSignificantPotential improvementIncrementalTransformative
The 80/20 Rule
If current tool serves 80% of needs, the 80% improvement from switching rarely justifies the 100% cost of migration. The last 20% isn’t worth the switch cost unless it’s blocking critical functionality.
Anti-Pattern Warning
See Anti-Pattern - Tool Overfocus — switching tools as optimization is different from switching as procrastination. If you’re constantly evaluating alternatives, the tool isn’t the problem.
Migration Principles

Export first — Always verify export works before committing
Selective migration — Not everything survives; prune aggressively
Reorganization opportunity — Migration is a chance to restructure, not just port
Test period — Run both tools in parallel for 2-4 weeks

Test Criteria (for AI Evaluation)

 Is the current tool actually blocking a core workflow?
 Have you used the current tool consistently for 6+ months?
 Can you name 3 specific features missing from current tool?
 Does new tool solve those 3 specifically?
 Have you tested new tool for 2+ weeks before migrating?

Types of Applicability Boundaries

Categorization of how knowledge boundaries can be documented

Knowledge doesn’t apply in different ways. Categorizing these boundary types helps capture when knowledge fails.
Why This Matters

Preventing misapplication: Knowledge correct in one context can cause harm in another.
Building trust: A KB that admits limitations is more trustworthy.
Saving time: Don’t try approaches known to fail for your situation.

An AI building a gardening KB with current Seed rules would tag with hardiness zones but miss: “this doesn’t work with clay soil,” “don’t combine with that fertilizer,” “fails above 90% humidity.”
Proposed Seed Rule

Rule: Document applicability boundaries — explicitly note when knowledge doesn’t apply.
Why: Knowledge works in one context, fails in another. Explicit boundaries prevent misapplication.
Test: Pick 5 notes with absolute language. Document when each doesn’t apply.

1. Contextual Boundaries
Knowledge that works in one context but not another:

“This pruning technique works for fruit trees, not ornamental”
“This teaching method works for beginners, not advanced learners”
“This financial advice applies to employees, not business owners”

2. Boundary Conditions
Knowledge correct at certain scales or thresholds:

“Newtonian physics works at everyday speeds, not at relativistic speeds”
“Linear regression works when relationships are linear, not for curved data”
“This recipe serves 4, not scalable below 2 servings”

3. Precondition Boundaries
Knowledge requiring specific conditions:

“This solution works only when you have X equipment”
“This approach requires Y amount of time”
“This advice applies only if you have Z background”

4. Temporal Boundaries
Knowledge correct but conditions changed:

“This worked in 2020 market conditions, not in 2024”
“Pre-pandemic travel advice no longer applies”
“This tool was free, now it’s subscription-only”

5. Combinatorial Boundaries
Knowledge failing when combined with other things:

“X and Y both work separately, but not together”
“This medication interacts with these other drugs”
“These two frameworks conflict when used simultaneously”

Structure Template
applicability:
  applies-to: [list where it works]
  does-not-apply-to: [list where it doesn't]
  boundary-conditions:
    - condition: "What must be true"
      threshold: "Break point"
  preconditions:
    required: [what's needed]
    incompatible: [what conflicts]
Related

The Inverse Test — Technique for finding undocumented boundaries

Wikilinks.title: Wikilinks
Wikilinks.content:
Wikilinks
Wikilinks (also called internal links or bidilinks) are inline links using double square bracket syntax: [[Atomic Note Principle]]. They are the primary connection mechanism in this vault.
Syntax Reference

























TypeSyntaxRenders AsDirect[[Atomic Note Principle]]Atomic Note PrincipleWith label[[Linking Principle|Connection Quality]]Connection QualitySectionNote Title (example syntax)Graph Traversal Efficiency → MCP Tools Reference
Why Wikilinks Over Markdown Links

No IDs needed — Link by title, not by arbitrary identifier
Auto-complete — Tools suggest existing notes as you type
Refactoring friendly — Rename a note, links update automatically
Readable source — Graph Traversal Efficiency is clearer than [Note 123](./notes/note-123.md)
Bidirectional by default — Most tools show backlinks automatically

This aligns with the Seed rule requiring flat file structure with wikilinks — no nested folders.
Creating Links Effectively
The “Create as You Link” Pattern
When you write a wikilink to a note that doesn’t exist (e.g., New Note Name as an example):

Most tools prompt to create it
This encourages incremental note creation
Prevents “note hoarding” where ideas are saved but never turned into notes

Link Text Matters

















PreferAvoid[[Atomic Note Principle]]ANP (unclear abbreviation - don’t use)[[note-naming-conventions|Naming]] for varietySame link text repeated
When NOT to Link

Decorative use just to add links
Keyword matches without conceptual connection
Forcing links to meet a quota (quality over quantity)

See Linking Principle for the “why follow?” test every link should pass.
Wikilinks and Graph Structure
Wikilinks create the knowledge graph:

Forward links: Notes this note points to
Backlinks: Notes that point to this note
Together they form navigable paths

The Seed requires every note be reachable from _root in 3 hops or fewer. Wikilinks make this possible through:

Hub notes (Hub Node Creation)
Dense but meaningful connections (Graph Traversal Efficiency)

Tool Support
Most modern knowledge management tools support wikilinks:

Obsidian, Logseq, RemNote — Native support
Roam Research — Uses double bracket syntax
Quartz, Obsidian Publish, Logseq Publish — Static site generators parse wikilinks

This vault’s Graph Traversal Efficiency can query the link structure programmatically.
Best Practices Summary

Use descriptive titles: [[Atomic Note Principle]] not abbreviations
Create notes as you link — if it doesn’t exist, make it
Bidirectional is automatic — most tools show backlinks
Test every link with the “why follow?” test from Linking Principle
Avoid over-linking — each link should add genuine value

Handling Edge Cases
Broken Links
When a linked note is deleted or renamed:

Don’t ignore broken links — They indicate missing knowledge or outdated references
Use deprecation pattern — Replace with a note explaining what happened
Search before creating — Verify the note doesn’t already exist under a different name

Alias Patterns
Use aliases to avoid duplicate notes:
# This note covers the same topic as [[note-naming-conventions]]
# Use this canonical note instead
This prevents fragmentation when the same concept has multiple names.
Link Text Diversity
While consistency matters, vary link text to avoid repetition:

First use: [[Atomic Note Principle]]
Later mentions: the atomicity principle, that note on single ideas

Case Sensitivity
Most wikilink implementations are case-insensitive but title-sensitive:

[[Atomic Note Principle]] and [[Atomic Note Principle]] typically resolve to the same note
[[Atomic Note Principle]] and [[Atomic Note Principle]] may be different
Use consistent casing matching the target note’s title

Related

Linking Principle — Quality criteria for meaningful connections
Note Insertion Strategy — Where to add new linked notes
Graph Traversal Efficiency — Navigation within 3 hops
Hub Node Creation — When to create navigation hubs
Graph Maintenance — Keeping the graph healthy
Emergence in Knowledge Graphs — How connections create emergent insights

Writing-as-Thinking.title: Writing as Thinking
Writing-as-Thinking.content:
Writing as Thinking
Writing is not just recording — it’s a tool for thinking itself.
The Difference

























RecordingThinkingTranscribing what you readProcessing what you readPassive captureActive engagement”What did they say?""What do I think?”StorageUnderstanding
Why Writing Think

Clarifies ideas - You don’t truly understand something until you explain it
Creates connections - Writing forces you to find links to existing knowledge
Generates new ideas - The act of writing reveals insights you’d miss just reading
Enables emergence - Combining notes in writing creates new concepts

The Feynman Technique
Explain a concept simply — if you can’t, you don’t understand it well enough. Named after physicist Richard Feynman, who famously used this method to explain complex physics concepts.
1. Choose a concept
2. Write as if teaching it to someone else
3. Identify gaps in your explanation
4. Fill gaps with research
5. Simplify and clarify

In Your Knowledge Base

Don’t just save — process (see Progressive Summarization)
Write notes in your own words
Ask: “What’s my take on this?”
Let notes evolve through writing

Zettelkasten-Method.title: Zettelkasten Method
Zettelkasten-Method.content:
Zettelkasten Method
The Zettelkasten (German for “slip box”) method is a foundational approach to networked knowledge management.
Origin
Developed by Niklas Luhmann, a German sociologist who wrote 70+ books and 400+ academic articles using only his Zettelkasten.
Core Philosophy

Atomic notes — One idea per note
Unique IDs — Each note has a unique identifier for direct addressing
Linking — Notes connect to related notes, forming a web of knowledge

How It Works
graph LR
    A[Idea 1] --> B[Atomic Note 1]
    C[Idea 2] --> D[Atomic Note 2]
    B --> D[Links to]
    D --> B[Backlinks]
    B --> E[Atomic Note 3]
    E --> D

The Luhmann Principle

“I do not think for myself, I let my Zettelkasten think for me.”

The system becomes a thinking partner that generates insights through connections.
The Numbering Myth
Common misconception: Zettelkasten uses sequential IDs (1, 1a, 1b, 1b1…)
Reality: Luhmann used links, not IDs. The ID system was a later interpretation.
The Essential Rules (Luhmann)

Write one idea per note
Write in your own words
Link notes together
Add permanent notes sequentially
Never delete - only deprecate

Modern Adaptation
We use wikilinks instead of IDs:
Concept instead of "Note 1a"

This is actually closer to Luhmann’s original method than the ID system.
Key Differences from Traditional Notes

























TraditionalZettelkastenHierarchical foldersNetwork of linksNotes stand aloneNotes are interconnectedHard to find connectionsGraph reveals connectionsNotes get lostEvery note is discoverable
Our Implementation
We use Atomic Note Principle and Linking Principle to implement Zettelkasten digitally.

git-best-practices.title: git-best-practices
git-best-practices.content:
Git Best Practices for Knowledge Bases

This note covers git practices specifically for maintaining AI-assisted knowledge bases. For general git usage, refer to external git documentation.

AI Agent Workflow
When AI agents make changes to the knowledge base:
Automated Commits
AI agents should commit after each meaningful change:

New note added → commit with [Add] Note title
Link added between notes → commit with [Link] Note A → Note B
Note updated → commit with [Improve] Note title
Fix broken link → commit with [Fix] Broken link in Note

Commit Message Format
[Type] Brief description

- Added: [new node/link]
- Fixed: [issue]
- Improved: [change]

Types: Add, Fix, Refactor, Improve, Document, Merge, Delete
File Naming for AI Agents
AI agents should use consistent naming:

Use kebab-case.md for filenames
Spaces in titles become hyphens: Atomic Note Principle.md → atomic-note-principle.md
This ensures predictable file paths for graph tools

Excluded Files
AI agents must never commit generated files:

.mcp-cache/ - Graph index cache
.obsidian/ - Editor settings
*.log - Log files
Build artifacts (public/, dist/)

Related

AI-Assisted Knowledge Management Seed
Self-Improvement Cycle
Graph Maintenance

Test Criteria

 Do AI agents use consistent commit types?
 Are filenames in kebab-case?
 Are cache files in .gitignore?
 Does each commit represent one logical change?
